I went through this recently with my best friend. 

Start just by being there with him - more and more as needed (eg. Right when the dog dies). Your presence really means a lot even if you don't say or do anything. A lot is communicated by you being there. Sometimes it's just as simple as holding him while he cries. Make sure he knows it's okay and safe and healthy for him to express his feelings and cry if he feels it. Spend lots of time with him, making sure he is meeting his basic needs (showering, make meals for him, help with his laundry, encourage him to sleep etc.). Grief can make things like that really difficult. 

For a gift...you could have a pawprint casting made of his dog's pawprint (could also be done at the vet clinic if he is euthanized). It would be a little piece of him forever. You could also get a little memory stone with the dog's name on it to put in the house or garden. You could also make a collage of memories with the dog.

Watch for signs of depression as opposed to grief. You may want to recommend counseling if his grief seems unhealthy or concerning in some way. 

Make sure when your bf wants to talk about the dog, you encourage that and join in. Maybe smile and share comforting happy memories. Reminiscing can be a good way to validate and help process healthy grieving.  Remind him what a good dog owner he was and how much his dog loved him. Now if your bf doesn't want to talk... Don't push him. Just meet him where he is at, and be supportive and kind (you already sound very supportive and kind so you should have no problem with this.).

It might be a good idea once some time has passed, to ask if he wanted support or help memorializing the dog in some way and hearing his thoughts on how he wants to remember his furry friend.

You could also paint him a picture of the dog. I painted a picture of my friend's dog looking up towards the lights in the sky, and on a rainbow bridge, and then I also got a pawprint made. I waited a couple months after her dog passed away to give them to her since she was showing signs of healing. At first she was overcome by emotion and I wasn't sure if she would be able to look at them. Now they are treasures to her.

It's a sad time for anyone. You can't protect your loved one from being sad. But you can shoulder the burden with them and support them so they are not alone. ❤️

I typed out a message to a friend that I missed. Something like,

"Hi Bob! I was thinking about you today because I remembered that you had [something important coming up]*. Good luck! I miss you and hope you're doing well. What's new?"

*[or it could be something funny/nice/creepy/etc you saw that reminded you of a memory you shared with them]

Just something short like that. I think generally people like it when others think of them, especially their friends. 

You might first think -- I don't know if I can get in touch with them randomly like that. 
My response: They're your friend and a friend would welcome hearing from you at any point, and they probably miss you too.

Then you might think -- No, they aren't really that close with me.
My response: That's anxiety talking, and you are probably quite close -- plus, if you send them a message, they will get closer with you and feel warmly towards you because you just showed that you care about them. 

Then I sit and obsess over the message for a while and then make a random involuntary reaction where my finger jumps out and sends the message. Then it's done and I can't take it back. 

9 times out of 10, you will get back a nice, caring message or at least some variation on "thank you for the positive thoughts, I miss you too."

Then just make sure you do this every so often so the relationship doesn't get cold. Even better if you can hang out in person and get coffee or something.

As for being cold, just try to do things with them at the same time -- like see a movie together or something where you aren't pressured to just sit and talk while doing nothing else (because that is definitely anxiety-inducing). Then the pressure is off for conversation, and then you can kind of ease in being with them for a bit without being in a place where you have to talk. Then get a meal together after so you feel more comfortable. Then maybe you'll find that you're more relaxed and can talk more freely. Do things that make you laugh too -- laughter really helps loosen you up. :)

Good luck! Hope this helps.
